<reason>A wins by distinguishing smoother government payments from greater lasting welfare. B established a genuine stabilization advantage, but A directly accepted fluctuating dividends and explained how debt repayment and productive investments survive the downturn. A also exposed B’s unequal governance assumptions and the trade-off between adequate benefits now and preserving principal. B’s closing treated payout sufficiency as merely fund design and zero new payments as effectively zero protection, leaving A’s central comparison unanswered. B remained competitive on macroeconomic smoothing, but A handled the decisive pressure more convincingly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s response to B’s debt argument was decisive: repayment need not repeat because extinguished interest obligations remain extinguished. Combined with the distinction between steady and sufficient payouts, this undermined B’s claim that recurring fund payments necessarily provide better protection through a bust.</best_rebuttal>
